THE DATA PROVENANCE INITIATIVE, BY NAME, ON GOOGLE'S AI OVERVIEW, SIGNED OUT, 2026-10-29: 'a multi-institutional research project—led in part by researchers from MIT—that audits the datasets, licenses, and web domains used to train artificial intelligence models.' Four platforms (the Data Provenance Explorer over 1,800+ datasets, a Web Consent Explorer, Open Model Evolution, an AI Observatory) and three findings (license omission over 70% and error over 50% on hosting platforms, closed datasets concentrated in creative tasks and lower-resource languages, a rise of non-commercial licences driven by synthetic data). Four cards: the initiative's home page ('4,000+ audited datasets; 14,000 tracked web domains'), the arXiv paper, MIT Sloan, Nature Machine Intelligence (1,858 datasets across 44 collections).

Reading

The innocent reading first. The Overview identifies the project, lists its tools and reports what its audits found, from its own site, its paper and the press.

Findings
  • THE FINDINGS RIGHT. 'license omission of 70%+ and error rates of 50%+' is the record's quote from the founding paper. (Repaired 2026-10-29: the finding had given the README as its source.) Checked 2026-10-29 against the provenance census record of the same day and the sources it saved.
  • THE OPERATOR. The record quotes the initiative's own description, 'a multi-disciplinary volunteer effort'; the composition's 'led in part by researchers from MIT' follows the MIT Sloan card, and 'multi-institutional' is in no card. The record names the founding paper's authors (Shayne Longpre and 16 others); the composition names no one.
  • THE RECORD AT TOO COARSE A GRAIN. The record has one explorer and the first release's count (44 collections, 1,800+ datasets). The home-page card gives four platforms and '4,000+ audited datasets; 14,000 tracked web domains'. The /non row read dataprovenance.org the same day: 'Four public measurement systems' (the Data Provenance Explorer, the Web Consent Explorer, Open Model Evolution, the AI Observatory) and '4,000+ / datasets audited', '14,000 / web domains tracked'. The card's figures hold; the record is to carry them with their quotes.
  • THE NEGATIVE TAGS. 'NOT legal advice' and 'describing a collection does not establish which model used it' are not composed; the composition does not claim otherwise.
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

As with the revived Papers with Code on the MMRS side, the composition is ahead of the record on the entity's current extent: the census formalized the initiative from its first release and its repository, and the Overview read its present home page. The capture is a correction to be made from the entity's own page.

Inline links are Google redirect URLs, kept as pasted.] [QUERENT] Data Provenance Initiative [SYSTEM] The [Data Provenance Initiative](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESVwHrOzAVIs_bBUxr7ducYJKxi6mO2H8PFkOqeMYxYB9BZOGggLJumXN31RQqX2ghNJ2wlF1SU0MHuuvc_7Cgibm_RylNPmv9oYEqoRYseVd3oqu3XZKm1g) is a multi-institutional research project—led in part by researchers from MIT—that audits the datasets, licenses, and web domains used to train artificial intelligence models. [[1], [2]] Key Tools & Platforms * Data Provenance Explorer: An interactive tool that audits and filters over 1,800+ text and fine-tuning datasets across dozens of collections to inspect sources, lineages, and license types. * Web Consent Explorer: A system that tracks thousands of web domains for consent signals and web policies. * Open Model Evolution: A monitor tracking open-source and open-weight AI models for transparency and concentration. * AI Observatory: A comparative tool for analyzing real-world AI conversation sets. [[1], [2], [3]] Major Findings from Audits * License Omission & Errors: Widely used hosting platforms exhibit over a 70% license omission rate and more than 50% error rates in how they categorize dataset licenses. [1] * Composition Divides: Commercially closed or restrictive datasets often monopolize creative tasks, specialized topics, and lower-resource languages. [1] * Non-Commercial Spikes: There has been a significant rise in non-commercial and academic-only licenses, frequently driven by synthetic data generated via commercial APIs. [1] Would you like to explore how to use the Data Provenance Explorer, or look into specific dataset licenses? Data Provenance Initiative Data Provenance Initiative
